Undefined named references also come from copy-pasting a passage out of another document, and a reference list the body never cites can be a deliberate further-reading section. Judge the cluster: plausible-but-invented names alongside markup faults and citation plumbing that does not connect. Escaped quotes are also normal inside JSON and shell strings, where the escaping is real syntax. Humans make the same mistakes: new users do not know the naming rules, and returning editors remember categories that were deleted while they were away. Check earlier revisions, because a reviewer may already have removed the broken ones. No regex separates an invented category from a real one, so the category sub-form is a reader's check on whether the category exists. A named reference is the recommended way to reuse a citation, and it only becomes evidence when it arrives with transport-escaped quotes.

artifacts.name: Stale or implausible boilerplate metadata
artifacts.definition: A new document arrives carrying metadata it could not have earned: maintenance, protection or style templates dated before the document existed ('{{Use American English|date=September 2022}}' on a 2025 creation), a submission header that pre-declines the submission ('{{AfC submission|d}}', whose 'd' parameter means declined, so the creator then asks why it was declined with no feedback), and access dates a year or more older than the work because the model's notion of 'today' is stale. The mechanism is boilerplate lifted from training examples plus a knowledge-cutoff date leaking into a metadata field.
cues: an access-date a year or more before the page was created, repeated across several citations on the same stale date

examples.before: A page created in February 2025 opening with {{Use American English|date=September 2022}}
examples.after: A page created in February 2025 opening with {{Use American English|date=February 2025}}

examples.before: {{AfC submission|d}} on a draft nobody has reviewed
examples.after: {{AfC submission}} on a draft nobody has reviewed

merged_from: Implausible pre-placed maintenance or protection templates
artifacts.false_positives: Copied citations, offline work and batch moves or merges all produce old access dates honestly; the tell is a set of them clustered on one stale date. A dated template that matches the document's own history is ordinary maintenance, and newer chatbots seldom get the date wrong at all. Check the page history before calling a banner implausible, and check who inserted it.

artifacts.name: Instructions and notes to the person publishing the text
artifacts.definition: Text addressed to whoever will paste, submit or review the document, published inside it. Sub-forms: numbered submission notes ('Submit via WP:AFC, not directly to mainspace', 'Declare COI in the edit summary'), a line telling the handler to remove the note ('Delete this section before submission'), coaching on what to say if a reviewer objects, a checklist of what the subject should have 'before creating a real page', a cover letter arguing the document's merits to a reviewer ('Reviewer note: this draft is neutral and well-sourced ... Thank you for your review'), and editorial suggestions about the document written in its own register ('Including photos of the forge would enrich the article's section on culture', 'a map could be added to orient readers', 'could further engage readers'). Often hidden inside HTML comments, so scan comment blocks as well. None of it is content.
cues: Before creating a real Wikipedia page
To have a good chance of acceptance, your
This article should be created at
convert as many items as possible in the citation list into inline references
could be added to orient readers
could be illustrated with an image
Several such photographs are available (e.g., on Wikimedia Commons)
would also add depth to the article
the expanded article can provide a richer, more immersive picture
This draft is a neutral and well-sourced biography
All references are from independent, reliable sources

examples.before: Delete this section before submission. After pasting the article, convert the citation list into inline references.
examples.after: (deleted; the article starts at its first line)

examples.before: Including photos of the forge would enrich the article's section on culture, and a map could be added to orient readers.
examples.after: (moved to the talk page as a suggestion, over the editor's own signature)

merged_from: Submission notes and instructions to the paster
Editorial advice about the article, inside the article
artifacts.false_positives: A style guide, a contributing guide, a runbook or a README is instructions on purpose. An editorial note in something explicitly marked as a draft, or in a review thread, a ticket or a PR description, is doing its job; the tell is process instruction inside the finished artefact, addressed to its handler rather than its reader. Note also that advice of this kind is often wrong on the facts, so removing it loses nothing.

artifacts.name: Self-certification of compliance
artifacts.definition: The text asserts its own neutrality, sourcing or rule-conformance instead of demonstrating it: 'Written to Wikipedia Manual of Style. Neutral tone, sourced throughout.', 'ensure that the content is presented in a neutral tone, supported by reliable sources', 'We remain committed to creating content that aligns with the mission'. The change-note form stacks verbose, unspecific assurances across a range of improvements nobody would bundle ('for clarity and compliance with the Manual of Style', 'corrected promotional wording, improved sourcing and neutrality'). The AI-disclosure form pre-empts the objection ('I understand concerns regarding AI-generated content, and I worked to ensure it adheres to the rules', 'these comments reflect my own thoughts'). Delete the claim and let the text carry it.
cues: Written to Wikipedia Manual of Style
We remain committed to creating content that aligns with Wikipedia's mission
presented in a neutral tone, supported by reliable sources
I understand (that) my [contributions] may [have been] perceived as
to ensure the article adheres to Wikipedia's
for clarity and compliance with the Manual of Style
regex: \bin compliance with (?:wikipedia|the platform|the manual of style|the guidelines|the style guide)\b

examples.before: Revised the section for clarity and compliance with the Manual of Style; corrected promotional wording and improved sourcing and neutrality.
examples.after: removed excessive links per MOS:OVERLINK

examples.before: This draft is written to the Manual of Style. Neutral tone, sourced throughout.
examples.after: (deleted; the draft's sources are listed under References)

examples.before: I understand concerns regarding AI-generated content; the page was rewritten in compliance with the manual of style.
examples.after: (deleted; the disputed sentence now carries a source)

merged_from: Downplaying AI use by claiming effort to ensure compliance (WP:AIMADEBUTSTILLOK)
Canned assurance of adherence to policies and guidelines (edit summaries)
artifacts.false_positives: A human citing one rule, briefly and with a link ('removed excessive links per MOS:OVERLINK'), is normal practice, and a common abbreviation such as 'ce' for copy edit is not a chatbot. A compliance statement a process actually requires (an accessibility statement, a licence header, a declared conflict of interest) is content. The tell is unspecific assurance stacked several deep, covering improvements nobody would bundle in one pass. The move transfers to any venue with a rulebook, so the English wording of the cues is an instance rather than the limit. Templated-change-note covers the neighbouring case, an edit summary written as exhaustive procedural prose; 'for a more neutral tone' is scored there alone so one summary does not report twice. What this entry scores is the assurance of rule-conformance itself, wherever it sits, including in the body or on a talk page.

artifacts.name: The brief's vocabulary and the destination named inside the deliverable
artifacts.definition: The output echoes the wording of the criteria it was asked to satisfy, or names the venue it was written for, from inside the text. Sub-forms: guideline vocabulary collapsed into the product ('These sources provide significant, substantial, secondary coverage, not trivial mentions or press releases'); the destination named with a possessive and a rule noun ('adheres to Wikipedia's guidelines on verifiability and neutrality', 'the Animal Cruelty Controversy section of Foshan's Wikipedia page'); rule shortcodes glossed for the reader ('Submit via WP:AFC (Articles for Creation)'). Somebody writing in place does not spell out where they are or which rulebook they read. Cut the frame; the text already sits where it sits. The rubric form is the same move in schoolwork and grant writing: the prompt's checklist reappears as the piece's structure and vocabulary, showing the generator was handed the criteria and optimised against them instead of doing the work.
cues: not trivial mentions or press releases
Wikipedia's guidelines on verifiability and neutrality
Post to WP:COIN (Conflict of Interest Noticeboard)
Before creating a real Wikipedia page
It meets WP:RS and WP:BLP standards and demonstrates clear notability per WP:NBIO through:

examples.before: These sources provide significant, substantial, secondary coverage, not trivial mentions or press releases.
examples.after: (deleted from the article; the sources are cited where they support a sentence)

examples.before: Ensure the content is presented in a neutral tone and adheres to Wikipedia's guidelines on verifiability.
examples.after: (deleted; the passage now attributes each contested claim to its source)

examples.before: This essay demonstrates critical engagement with the source material, uses evidence effectively, and maintains a coherent structure throughout.
examples.after: Milgram's 1963 obedience results do not survive Perry's archival findings, and section three works through why.

merged_from: Guideline or justification vocabulary collapsed into the deliverable
Explicit destination self-reference and policy name-dropping
artifacts.false_positives: A discussion about whether a subject qualifies is exactly where guideline vocabulary belongs, and citing one rule with a link in a review or a change note is normal; the tell is that vocabulary inside the deliverable. Documentation that names its own platform because the platform is the subject is fine, as is a style guide quoting its own criteria. The Wikipedia instances are the reported case, and the mechanism transfers to any brief, so a blog post that says 'for this blog' or a PR that recites the contributing guidelines is the same move. Students are taught to signpost against the rubric, and grant applications and tender responses are required to mirror the criteria section by section; flag when the criteria vocabulary appears in place of the content it was meant to measure. 'Independent coverage' is two words of ordinary editorial English that any sourcing review will use correctly, so it is kept as a cue with no regex behind it.

artifacts.name: Templated change note (commit message, PR description, edit summary)
artifacts.definition: A change description written as exhaustive procedural prose rather than a terse human note. Sub-forms: the full-sentence summary of everything done and how it complies ('Improved clarity, flow, and readability of the plot section; reduced redundancy and refined tone for better encyclopedic style'); the statement of what was deliberately not changed, which echoes the prompt's constraint back ('while preserving the original meaning and technical details', 'while maintaining backward compatibility'); the enumeration of every field, parameter or template touched with its literal syntax ('Corrected infobox parameters (image_size)'); and the older first-person form carrying the same tells as the body text, with AI vocabulary, emoji or Markdown in the summary itself ('**Concise edit summary:** I revised the content to...'). The more rigidly formulaic, the stronger the sign.
cues: reduced redundancy and refined tone for better encyclopedic style
while preserving the original meaning and technical details
preserved existing structure and lead emphasis
The tone was adjusted to be more encyclopedic and less promotional

examples.before: Improved clarity, flow, and readability of the plot section; reduced redundancy and refined tone for better encyclopedic style.
examples.after: ce plot

examples.before: Removed promotional language and revised the passage for a neutral tone while preserving the original meaning and technical details.
examples.after: drop marketing adjectives from the throughput claim

merged_from: Older-style edit summary: first person, AI vocabulary, emoji, list or Markdown formatting
Overemphasis on parameter, template and markup names
artifacts.false_positives: A long, specific change note that says what changed and why, with links, is good practice: length and formality are not the tell, the formula is. Conventional-commit bodies, changelogs and release notes are meant to enumerate. 'While maintaining backward compatibility' is worth saying once, when it is the point of the change; the tell is the same constraint echoed on every commit. The further a summary deviates from the formula, the less likely it is generated, and a summary written by hand for a generated change is rare enough to ignore. Self-certification-of-compliance covers the neighbouring case, a change note that asserts its own neutrality or rule-conformance; read the two together on one edit summary and report it once.

artifacts.name: Letter register on a surface that is not correspondence
artifacts.definition: Business-letter framing on a ticket, a talk page, a comment, a form or an article: 'Dear Editorial Team,', 'I hope this message finds you well', 'I am writing to request an edit', 'Thank you for your understanding and assistance in this matter', 'Best regards,'. The register is right in an actual letter; the tell is its arrival where nobody writes letters, and it usually travels with unfilled placeholders from the same paste.
cues: I hope this message finds you well
I trust this message finds you well
I am writing to express my deep concern
Thank you for your understanding and assistance in this matter
We hope to resubmit our work once these changes have been made

examples.before: Dear Wikipedia Editorial Team, I hope this message finds you well. I am writing to request an edit to the entry.
examples.after: The second paragraph gives the wrong founding year: the charter is dated 1924, not 1932.

merged_from: Letter and email register on non-correspondence surfaces
Formal-letter opener in a comment (Dear Wikipedia Editorial Team)
artifacts.false_positives: In an actual email, cover letter or formal complaint this is the correct register and predates chatbots by centuries. Judge by surface: a talk page, an issue, a code comment, a commit message, an article. Formality alone is not a tell, and a non-native speaker leaning on a letter template is not a chatbot. A first contact with a stranger may reasonably borrow the register anywhere.

artifacts.name: Duplicated section or paragraph
artifacts.definition: A section or paragraph repeats verbatim or near-verbatim inside the same piece, because the generator lost track of what it had already written: the same section emitted twice word for word, or paragraph 3 restated as paragraph 17 with the wording shuffled. Detect by paragraph hashing or n-gram overlap. Delete the copy, and check first whether one half carries a fact the other lost.

examples.before: The plant closed in 1998 after the parent group withdrew funding. [...] After the parent group withdrew funding, the plant closed in 1998.
examples.after: The plant closed in 1998 after the parent group withdrew funding.

artifacts.false_positives: A deliberate refrain, a summary that restates the lead, a legal notice repeated by requirement, and boilerplate that appears in every section by design are not duplication. Reference material where each entry repeats a stock sentence is the format. The tell is an exact or near-exact repeat that neither position needs, and it is less common in recent output than it was.

artifacts.name: Text that stops mid-sentence
artifacts.definition: The piece ends in the middle of a sentence or a section because generation hit a token limit and nobody continued it, or because the copy was truncated: 'Final important tip: The ~~~~ at the very end is Wikipedia markup that automatically'. Detect a final sentence with no terminal punctuation, ending on a function word or an auxiliary. Finish the sentence or cut back to the last complete one.
cues: last sentence has no terminal punctuation and ends on a function word or auxiliary (and, the, to, is, which, that)

examples.before: The ~~~~ at the very end is Wikipedia markup that automatically
examples.after: Four tildes at the end sign the post with your username and a timestamp.

artifacts.false_positives: Deliberate aposiopesis in fiction or quoted speech, a heading as the last line, a table or code block at the end, and a list whose items carry no terminal punctuation are all normal. A malformed local copy-paste and a partial copy from another document produce the same shape, so this shows the text is unfinished and says nothing about who wrote it.

artifacts.name: Zero-width and homoglyph bypass characters
artifacts.definition: Invisible or lookalike characters inserted to defeat AI detectors: zero-width space, non-joiner, joiner, word joiner and byte-order mark (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060, U+FEFF), and Cyrillic or Greek letters swapped in for Latin lookalikes (а е о р с х у к м н в т, ο Ο α Α ρ Ρ). Their presence means the text went through a humanizer or prompt-injection bypass tool. Strip the characters and retype the affected words from your own keyboard.
cues: [Ѐ-ӿͰ-Ͽ] swapped via CYRILLIC_LOOKALIKES / GREEK_LOOKALIKES (а е о р с х у к м н в т А Е О Р С Х У К М Н В Т ο Ο α Α ρ Ρ)

examples.before: dеlve (the e is Cyrillic U+0435, inside an otherwise Latin word)
examples.after: delve, retyped from your own keyboard

examples.before: deli​ver (a zero-width space sits between the i and the v)
examples.after: deliver, retyped from your own keyboard

artifacts.false_positives: A single stray zero-width character or a byte-order mark can come from Word, Notion, a CMS export or a file's own encoding, which is why the detector wants two or more before it counts; one ZWSP should never flip a verdict on its own. Genuine Cyrillic or Greek text, transliteration tables and linguistics examples contain those letters legitimately, and so does any multilingual document; the tell is a Cyrillic letter sitting inside an otherwise Latin word.

artifacts.name: Roleplay action markers
artifacts.definition: Asterisk-wrapped stage directions from chat roleplay left in prose: '*nods*', '*sighs*', '*sighs and looks away*', '*leans in*'. The inner phrase opens with a stage verb, which is what separates it from ordinary emphasis. Two or more in a document is the threshold, because a single pair of asterisks may be Markdown italics.

examples.before: *nods thoughtfully* The migration ran clean.
examples.after: The migration ran clean.

artifacts.false_positives: Markdown emphasis around a word that happens to be one of these verbs ('it *looks* fine') is not a stage direction, which is exactly why the threshold is two. Fiction, screenplays and chat fiction use stage directions on purpose. Double-asterisk bold is excluded by the lookarounds.

artifacts.name: Generator wrapper and speaker label around the deliverable
artifacts.definition: The transport envelope around the answer gets pasted with the payload. Sub-forms: a container directive opening the deliverable, ':::writing{variant="document" id="68427"}' with a random five-digit id, localised as ':::écriture{variante="document"}' and often closed by a bare ':::'; and a transcript speaker label naming the model ('Claude responded:', 'ChatGPT I revised the content to...') followed by the assistant's own commentary about the text it just produced. Delete the wrapper and the commentary and keep the payload.
cues: That last sentence is the killer
you're speaking their language and daring them to argue with it

examples.before:
:::writing{variant="document" id="68427"}
AK7 is a Belgian rapper.
examples.after: AK7 is a Belgian rapper.

examples.before: Claude responded: That last sentence is the killer. Comprehensive rewrite: early life sourced from the university roster.
examples.after: Rewrote the early-life section from the university roster.

merged_from: Chatbot name or 'X responded:' prefix leaking into output
artifacts.false_positives: Triple-colon container directives are real syntax in MyST, Docusaurus, pandoc and several static-site generators, so on those surfaces they are the format; the tell is the wrapper on a surface with no such syntax, carrying a random numeric id. Quoting a model by name in a piece about models ('ChatGPT said it could not answer') is reporting, and a transcript that is presented as a transcript keeps its speaker labels.

artifacts.name: Provenance signals outside the text
artifacts.definition: Evidence about how the text arrived rather than how it reads: the whole document appearing as a single paste event in the editor's version history, and an author's sudden shift to flawless or formal prose against their own baseline, especially where that baseline predates late 2022. Process evidence of this kind is more defensible than a detector score, and it is never on its own a reason to change a sentence.

examples.before: A 2,000-word section arrives in one paste, from an account whose other edits are two-line notes.
examples.after: (no text edit; ask the author how the section was written)

artifacts.false_positives: A single paste is often a draft written elsewhere, in a local editor, a notes app or another document. Writers code-switch to a formal register in some venues, and long-term AI users drift in parallel with the models, so a gradual change proves nothing; only a dramatic and otherwise unexplainable shift counts. Consistency with pre-2023 habits, the same boldface or the same list style, argues against AI. Never treat this as a defect in the prose. Permissions-gaming carries the cross-document twin of this signal, many benign rewrites across unrelated pages in quick succession, where the volume and the spread rather than any sentence are what shows.

artifacts.name: Throwaway rewrites to inflate a record
artifacts.definition: Many benign-looking, unconstructive AI rewrites across unrelated pages in quick succession, made to build an edit count or contribution record before pursuing a different goal. The individual edits look harmless; the volume, the spread and the timing are the signal.

examples.before: Forty small rewrites across forty unrelated articles in one evening, none changing a fact.
examples.after: Reviewed as a pattern rather than edit by edit, and raised with the contributor before any action.

merged_from: Permissions gaming with throwaway AI rewrites (WP:PGAME)
artifacts.false_positives: The inference runs one way only: rapid AI-assisted additions are not evidence of gaming, while a contributor already shown to be gaming permissions may well be using AI for the volume. Gnomes, typo-fixers and bot-assisted cleanup make many small edits legitimately. Newcomer enthusiasm looks the same from outside. This is evidence about a contributor's record rather than about any sentence, so like out-of-text-provenance-signal it never justifies a text edit. The two differ in reach: that entry reads how one document arrived, this one reads a pattern across unrelated pages.

translationese.name: Calqued prepositional periphrasis (about / through / in that / related to / based on / in order to)
translationese.definition: An English preposition phrase is rendered with a heavy periphrastic frame every time, where the target language marks the same relation with a plain particle, case or verb ending. Six lexical sub-forms in the Korean sources: 'about / regarding / concerning' as ~에 대해(서)/대하여 where the verb takes a direct object (X를 논의); 'through / via / by means of' as ~를 통해(서)/통하여 where instrumental ~로, ~해서 or ~함으로써 serve; 'in that / in the sense that' as ~라는 점에서 where a connective ~서 or ~라는 이유로 serves; 'related to / with regard to' as ~와 관련하여/관련된 where ~에 or genitive ~의 serves; 'based on' as ~에 기반하여 / ~을 바탕으로 where ~로 or a concrete verb (~을 보고) serves; 'in order to / for the purpose of' as ~을 위해 where the purpose endings ~려고, ~도록 or adnominal ~위한 serve. Each frame is native on its own, so the tell is density: three or more of one frame inside a paragraph. The transferable slot is any relational, instrumental or purpose preposition the model reaches for uniformly.

examples.before: AI 규제에 대해 논의할 필요가 있다
examples.after: AI 규제를 논의해야 한다

examples.before: 데이터 분석을 통해 효율을 높일 수 있다
examples.after: 데이터를 분석해서 효율을 높인다

examples.before: 비용을 절감하기 위해 공정을 바꿨다
examples.after: 비용을 줄이려고 공정을 바꿨다

merged_from: A-1 ~에 대하여/대해서 overuse (English 'about / regarding / concerning X' calque)
A-4 ~라는 점에서 (English 'in that / in the sense that / in terms of the fact that')
A-5 ~와 관련하여 / ~와 관련된 (English 'related to / in relation to / with regard to')
A-11 ~을 위해 purpose clauses overuse (English 'in order to / for the purpose of / for')
A-11 '~을 위해' 목적절 남발 (in order to)
translationese.false_positives: None of these frames is wrong in isolation, so a single use is never a finding; only repetition inside one paragraph is. The ban version of this rule was rejected on evidence: 최희경 (2016) measured ~를 통해 at 84.4 per unit in non-translated Korean against 42.1 in translated Korean, so native writers use it twice as often as translators, and it barely appeared in the AI corpus; the same holds for ~에 대해, which humans use about three times more than the AI corpus. Redistribute the surplus and keep one or two. Never flag adnominal ~위한 (고객을 위한 서비스): that beneficiary form is the recommended replacement, not the tell, which is why the purpose regex matches only 위해/위하여. 점에서 inside a fixed academic or legal formula stands. The regexes are Korean and are the only tested instances; do not port them to Dutch or English text, where the equivalent slot needs its own calibration.

translationese.name: '~에 있어(서)' frame (in terms of / when it comes to / with respect to)
translationese.definition: The frame ~에 있어(서) used to introduce a topic, premise or domain, as a literal rendering of English 'in X / in terms of / when it comes to / with respect to'. The native forms are the plain locative ~에서, a bare topic particle, or ~을 볼 때. Both sources rate it decisive on a single occurrence, unlike the density-gated frames in calqued-preposition-periphrasis; it often arrives together with a dummy-noun head (중요한 점은) that should collapse at the same time.

examples.before: 이 문제에 있어서 중요한 것은
examples.after: 이 문제에서 중요한 건

examples.before: 이에 있어서 중요한 점은
examples.after: 여기서 중요한 건

merged_from: A-3 ~에 있어(서) (English 'in X / in terms of / when it comes to' calque)
A-3 '~에 있어(서)' (in terms of / when it comes to)
translationese.false_positives: Bare '에 있어' is also the ordinary existential verb 있다 plus a connective: 집에 있어, 회의는 3시에 있어, and '그는 집에 있어서 못 왔다' ('he was at home, so he could not come') all contain the string and none is the frame. That is why only the ~에 있어서 form carries a regex and the bare form stays a prose cue, and why even the regexed form needs a read: if 있- is a real predicate with a locative subject, leave it. Quoted statute and contract language that fixes the phrase stands.

translationese.name: Double-marked passive (~되어진다 / ~지게 된다)
translationese.definition: Two passive or inchoative morphemes stacked on one verb (되어지다, 아/어/여지게 되다), so a passive is passivised again, usually because an English passive was rendered on top of a verb that was already passive in the target. Prefer the active; if the agent genuinely cannot be named, use one passive marker.

examples.before: 판단되어진다
examples.after: 판단된다

examples.before: 상황이 나빠지게 된다
examples.after: 상황이 나빠진다

examples.before: 이 문제는 곧 해결되어질 것이다
examples.after: 우리는 이 문제를 곧 해결한다

translationese.false_positives: -게 되다 on its own is native and means a change of state or an outcome outside the subject's control (그렇게 되었다, 가게 되었다), and the second regex deliberately matches the bare cue form 지게 되-, so a stem that simply ends in the syllable 지 (가지게 되다, 만지게 되다) matches too and is not this pattern: read the stem before flagging. The vowel-linked form -아/어/여지게 되- was tested as a tighter guard and rejected, because Korean contracts that vowel (나쁘다 becomes 나빠지다) and the guard then misses real instances. 되어지 has no legitimate use. Evidence anchor: 김혜영 (2009), a one-million-eojeol contrastive study, is the only Korean work with measured discriminative power, and syntactic passives are among its features.

translationese.name: Agentless automated passive (만들어지다 / 이루어지다)
translationese.definition: An event stated as something that 'was made' or 'was achieved' with a generic passive and no actor at all (합의가 이루어졌다, 'agreement was reached'), instead of the actor doing it. Distinct from stacked-double-passive (morphology) and from agentive-by-passive (the agent is named): here the agent has vanished and the verb is a colourless 'be made / be done'. Restore the agent and a plain active verb.

examples.before: 합의가 이루어졌다
examples.after: 양측이 합의했다

examples.before: 새로운 기준이 만들어졌다
examples.after: 위원회가 새 기준을 만들었다

merged_from: A-12 Automated passives 만들어지다 / 이루어지다 (English 'was made / was achieved / took place')
translationese.false_positives: 이루어지다 in the composition sense (X로 이루어져 있다, 'consists of') hides no agent and is native, which is why the regex refuses any of these verbs followed by 있 (the state reading). 만들어지다 is right for a product whose maker is irrelevant or unknown (이 치즈는 산에서 만들어진다). The tell is an event with a real, recoverable actor that the sentence declined to name. This needs document-level judgement, so the source marks it not-quick: check whether the actor appears anywhere nearby before rewriting.

translationese.name: Passive progressive (~되고 있다 / ~지고 있다) for 'is being ~ed'
translationese.definition: A trend or state described with the passive progressive ~되고 있다 / ~지고 있다, transferring English 'is being ~ed' and 'is increasingly ~ed', where a plain present or past tense carries the same claim. The tell is three or more in one paragraph, which turns every sentence of a trend passage into the same shape.

examples.before: 관심이 높아지고 있으며 투자도 확대되고 있다
examples.after: 관심이 높아졌고 투자도 늘었다

merged_from: A-20 피동 진행 '~되고 있다 / ~지고 있다' 남발 (passive progressive)
translationese.false_positives: A process genuinely under way right now takes this form in native Korean (눈이 내리고 있다, 공사가 진행되고 있다); the aspect is the point there, not a translation artifact. Only the repetition is the finding, and only where a simple tense would say the same thing. Do not convert a hedged in-progress claim into a completed one just to remove the shape, because that trades a style tell for a factual error.

translationese.name: Ability modal on every predicate (~할 수 있다 / can / could / be able to)
translationese.definition: Every predicate softened with the ability modal ~할 수 있다 because the English source said 'can / could / be able to': '효율을 높일 수 있다' where '효율을 높인다' is the claim actually being made. The tell is repetition, four or more identical uses in a stretch, flattening warranted assertions and genuine hedges into one shape. Where the claim is warranted, assert it in the plain tense; where it is not, keep the modality.

examples.before: 이 도구는 시간을 절약할 수 있다
examples.after: 이 도구는 시간을 절약한다

merged_from: A-10 ~할 수 있다 overuse (English modal 'can / could / be able to')
A-10 '~할 수 있다' 남발 (can / be able to)
translationese.false_positives: This is one of the most common native Korean constructions and a per-occurrence flag is noise; only four or more identical repeats in one stretch is the finding. The larger risk runs the other way: the source had to re-word this rule toward preservation because rewriters kept converting real epistemic modality into assertion ('낮은 것으로 판단된다' becoming '낮은 수치다'), and a restore_modality backstop was added to catch it. Ability, permission and genuine uncertainty all keep the modal. General reflexive hedging in English or Dutch copy is a different finding, scored by the baseline's hedging entries, not here.

translationese.name: English-style noun stacking with particles dropped
translationese.definition: A chain of bare nouns mirroring English noun-noun compounding (AI 기술 발전 속도 가속화, 'AI technology development speed acceleration'), with the particles that mark the relations between them left out, so the reader has to reconstruct the English to parse it. Restore the particles and a finite verb.

examples.before: AI 기술 발전 속도 가속화
examples.after: AI 기술의 발전 속도가 빨라지고 있다

merged_from: A-13 English-style noun stacking with particles dropped
A-13 명사 나열 (noun stacking, particle omission)
translationese.false_positives: Lexicalised technical compounds and proper names are native and must not be broken up (인공지능 기술 표준, 국가정보원). Headlines, table headers, slide titles and list labels drop particles by convention. The finding is a four-or-more chain in running prose whose internal relations are only recoverable from the English. No regex: the source cues are descriptive, not literal, and any surface pattern for 'bare nouns in a row' misfires badly in Korean. A Dutch adaptation must recalibrate rather than port this, because Dutch compounds natively and writes the chain as one word.

translationese.name: Clauses joined with a free conjunction ('그리고' as English 'And')
translationese.definition: Two clauses written as separate sentences and joined by the free conjunction 그리고, the way English coordinates with 'and', where the native form fuses them with a connective verb ending (-고, -며, -면서). The mechanism is English clause-level coordination imported into a language whose coordination is morphological.

examples.before: 그는 보고했다. 그리고 자리에 앉았다.
examples.after: 그는 보고하고 자리에 앉았다.

merged_from: A-14 그리고 joining clauses like English 'and'
A-14 접속부사 '그리고' 절 연결 ('and' clause linking)
translationese.false_positives: 그리고 between noun phrases in a list is native and is not this pattern, which is why the regex anchors on sentence-initial position. One deliberate sentence-initial 그리고 for rhythm or emphasis is a choice a human makes too; the finding is the habit, not the instance. Spoken-register transcripts and dialogue carry more of them legitimately.

translationese.name: Third-person pronoun over-translation (그 / 그녀 / 그것 / 그들 for he / she / it / they)
translationese.definition: Every English he, she, it and they rendered one-to-one as 그 / 그녀 / 그것 / 그들 in a language that normally drops the pronoun, producing three or more in a paragraph. Delete 50 to 70 percent, name the referent only at a speaker or scene change, and render 'they' as 사람들, 우리, 일부 or 어떤 이들. Fires only on text rendered or summarised from an English source.

examples.before: 그는 회의에 들어갔다. 그는 자료를 꺼냈고, 그것을 그들에게 보여주었다.
examples.after: 회의에 들어가 자료를 꺼내 참석자들에게 보여주었다.

merged_from: A-16 Third-person pronoun density 그/그녀/그것/그들 (1:1 mapping of he/she/it/they)
translationese.false_positives: Hard scope guard: on natively written Korean this is a false positive, and the numbers say so: humans used 그는/그의 more than the AI corpus (1.9 against 0.0 per 1000 eojeol), and the trigger event, three or more in a 200-character window, occurred in 3.9 percent of human texts against 0.7 percent of AI texts. Modern models suppress pronouns when writing Korean natively, so a pronoun chain is weak evidence of a machine and strong evidence of a human or a translation. Literary prose and translated fiction carry pronoun chains by design. The mechanism does not transfer to non-pro-drop languages such as Dutch and English; the only part that carries over is 'a pronoun where the target language would repeat the name at a scene change'.

translationese.name: Mechanical -들 plural marking on inanimate and abstract nouns (held)
translationese.definition: The obligatory English plural -s carried over as the plural suffix -들 on inanimate and abstract nouns, where the target language leaves number unmarked. This rule is on hold and must not fire: it has strong scholarly anchors but scored zero positives in both corpora, so it may be recorded as an observation and never named as a dominant pattern or prescribed as a rewrite.

examples.before: 정책들과 규제들이 논의되었다
examples.after: 정책과 규제를 논의했다

merged_from: A-17 Mechanical -들 plural marking on inanimate and abstract nouns (held)
A-17 무정물·추상명사 '-들' 복수 표지 (mechanical plural marker) [hold]
translationese.false_positives: Do not fire at all, because this is a held rule, kept so the pattern numbering stays stable and the deul_overuse_rate metric keeps measuring it, not so a scanner can flag it. Deliberately no regex. Even if it were active, -들 on animate nouns (학생들, 사람들) is obligatory, and -들 on inanimates is used for genuine emphasis or contrast in native Korean. Report it as an observation at most, and never as evidence a text is machine-written.

translationese.name: Left-branching pre-nominal modifier stack (relative clause of 3+ eojeol)
translationese.definition: An English post-nominal relative clause ('the X that ...') rendered as a long left-branching modifier in front of the head noun: three or more stacked adnominal phrases, or a modifier of three or more eojeol, so the reader holds the whole clause before learning what it modifies. Split the sentence, or postpose the clause as an apposition (X를 만났는데, 그 X는 ~).

examples.before: 지난해 유럽에서 발표된 새로운 규제를 반영한 보고서가 나왔다
examples.after: 보고서가 나왔다. 지난해 유럽에서 나온 새 규제를 반영한 것이다.

merged_from: A-18 Left-branching pre-nominal modifier / relative clause of 3+ eojeol
A-18 관계대명사절 직역 (left-branching relative clause stacking)
translationese.false_positives: Two stacked adnominals are ordinary Korean and the threshold is three; legal, academic and specification prose front-loads modifiers by convention and reads fine to its audience. No regex: the source cues are descriptive, and the metric behind them (relative_clause_nesting) is a parse depth rather than a string. A consecutive-adnominal proxy was written and then dropped, because a real stack separates its modifiers with their own objects (발표된 새로운 규제를 반영한 보고서) and the proxy misses exactly those while matching unrelated verb runs. The English-side analogue is comma-clause nesting, which the syntax category scores; do not double-count a sentence.

translationese.name: Stacked particles (~에서의 · ~에로의 · ~으로의 · ~에의 · ~으로부터의)
translationese.definition: A locative or directional particle followed by the genitive 의 (에서의, 에로의, 으로의, 에의, 으로부터의, 로부터의), mirroring English preposition-plus-'of' sequences ('the X of the Y in Z'), a shape Korean inherited from Japanese の and English prepositional phrases. Unfold the stack into a clause or a plain phrase.

examples.before: 국내에서의 논의는 유럽으로의 확산을 낳았다
examples.after: 국내 논의가 유럽으로 퍼졌다

merged_from: A-19 이중 조사 결합 (double particle combination)
translationese.false_positives: Plain ~의 on its own is explicitly not a target: there is no scholarly consensus on genitive overuse, and the source records that as an open caveat. Bare 로의 is left out of the regex on purpose, because a noun ending in the syllable 로 plus genitive 의 (도로의, 진로의, 통로의) is indistinguishable on the surface from the stacked particle. Fixed legal and bureaucratic collocations (에의 접근권) stand.

translationese.name: English gloss in parentheses repeated on every occurrence
translationese.definition: A term is followed by its English original in parentheses every time it appears, so 주권 AI(Sovereign AI) is followed later by 주권 AI(Sovereign AI) again rather than by the Korean term alone. The habit extends to glossing every technical term at once, so the page reads as a bilingual glossary. Gloss once, then use the target-language term alone.

examples.before: 주권 AI(Sovereign AI)는 국가 전략이다. 주권 AI(Sovereign AI) 정책은 예산을 요구한다.
examples.after: 주권 AI(Sovereign AI)는 국가 전략이다. 주권 AI 정책은 예산을 요구한다.

merged_from: B-1 Parenthetical English gloss repeated on every occurrence
B-1 괄호 병기 관습 (parenthetical English gloss habit)
translationese.false_positives: A first-mention gloss is correct practice and required in technical and academic writing; only the repeat is the finding, which is what the regex looks for (the same parenthetical returning within about 400 characters). A term whose English form is the conventional one in the field (API, SLA, CI) needs no gloss at all and is not this pattern. Glossaries, indexes, tables and reference lists repeat glosses by design. A parenthetical that adds new information rather than repeating a translation is not a gloss.

translationese.name: Whole English sentences quoted with a translation alongside
translationese.definition: A full English sentence is pasted verbatim into the body as a quotation and immediately followed by its translation, so the reader gets the same claim twice in two languages. It is the source text leaking through the generation. Unless the original wording itself matters, paraphrase in the target language and cite the source.
cues: 영어 문장을 인용문으로 그대로 박아넣고 번역도 병기

examples.before: 보고서는 “Adoption will accelerate over the next two years.”라고 적었다. (“도입은 앞으로 2년간 가속화될 것이다.”)
examples.after: 보고서는 도입이 앞으로 2년간 빨라질 것으로 봤다.

merged_from: B-3 Whole English sentences embedded as quotations with a translation alongside
B-3 과도한 영어 인용구 (excessive English quotations)
translationese.false_positives: The explicit exception is that the original wording genuinely matters: a term of art, a legal formula, a slogan under analysis, or a quotation whose exact phrasing is the subject of the sentence. Quote it once and cite it. Language-teaching material, bilingual documentation and translation commentary present both versions by design. A short English phrase or a product name inside a target-language sentence is not this pattern; the regex requires a quoted run of at least twenty-five Latin characters followed by Hangul, so it stays inert on English text.

translationese.name: 'Known as / so-called' appositive calque (~라고 알려진 / ~로 일컬어지는)
translationese.definition: The English appositive 'X, known as Y' or 'the so-called Y' rendered as a full relative construction (~라고 알려진, ~로 일컬어지는), where the target language writes the noun with a parenthetical abbreviation. It is a weak tell on its own and strengthens when it stacks with the other English-over-quoting habits.

examples.before: 'AGI'라고 알려진 범용 인공지능
examples.after: 범용 인공지능(AGI)

translationese.false_positives: When the naming is the point, because the thing genuinely goes by two names or the text is about who calls it what, the construction is doing real work and stays. 알려진 in the sense 'well known, famous' (잘 알려진 사실) is a different use. Rated weak on its own by the source, so a single instance is not a finding; it counts when it appears alongside repeated parenthetical glosses or embedded English quotations.

translationese.name: Interference index (composite metric over the A-class signals)
translationese.definition: A metric, not a sentence-level pattern: Toury's (1995) interference axis operationalised as nine measurable signals combined into one index: inanimate_subject_rate (abstract-subject-all-purpose-verb), by_passive_count and double_passive_count (the three passive entries), pronoun_density (pronoun-over-translation), deul_overuse_rate (mechanical-plural-marking, held), relative_clause_nesting (left-branching-modifier-stack), have_make_literal_count (light-verb-literalism), double_particle_count (stacked-particles) and progressive_aspect_rate (passive-progressive-calque). It is the structural map of this whole category: the nine axes are what a non-Korean adaptation refills with its own instances. Linkage runs both ways: pattern counts over threshold drive the diagnosis, and a composite off baseline triggers extra verification at finalize.

examples.before: 이 보고서에 의해 도출되어진 결과들은 정책 결정에 있어서 활용될 수 있다
examples.after: 연구진은 이 결과를 정책 결정에 쓴다

merged_from: Post-editese: interference index (metric-only, composite of A-class signals)
translationese.false_positives: Never report this as a finding on a sentence: it is a document-level score, and the source marks it speculative and deliberately unnumbered. A high index on a text that actually is a translation is expected and is not a defect. Two of its nine inputs are themselves constrained (deul_overuse_rate feeds a held rule that must not fire, and pronoun_density is valid only in translation contexts), so the index is a trigger for a closer look, not evidence on its own.

translationese.name: Untranslated English marketing buzzword in a non-English text
translationese.definition: English marketing adjectives and verbs (seamless, robust, leverage, scalable, synergy, holistic) dropped untranslated and unexplained into a target-language sentence, breaking its rhythm and reading as display. Render marketing words in the target language, and keep standard technical terms in the original, which is the counter-rule.

examples.before: 이 도구는 seamless한 경험을 제공합니다.
examples.after: 이 도구는 끊김 없는 경험을 제공합니다.

merged_from: B-2 Unexplained marketing buzzwords left in English
B-2 불필요한 영어 장식·일회성 jargon (buzzword decoration)
translationese.false_positives: Never mechanically translate established technical terms: API, prompt, token and pipeline stay in the original, and rendering 'prompt' as 지시문 is the error this rule is most often misapplied to produce. A loanword that has entered the target language as ordinary vocabulary is not a hit. Quoted English, product names and brand taglines are exempt. The regex only fires where the English word sits directly against CJK or Hangul text, so it is inert on English prose.
